title: Gold coins on the ground
hook: Anathapindika covers Prince Jeta's grove with gold coins to buy it for the monks (Vinaya, Cullavagga 6)

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the women of the first sangha: founders, teachers, mothers, queens. Your line was she taught too. Who came to mind? Today the lay followers begin, starting with a merchant and his carts of gold. Day seven hundred sixty-seven.

A merchant from Savatthi arrives in Rajagaha on business and finds his brother-in-law's house in an uproar. Cooking for a crowd, servants rushing about. Is there a wedding? Has the king been invited? No, says the brother-in-law. The Buddha and his monks are coming for a meal tomorrow. The merchant stops at that word, Buddha. He meets the teacher, hears him, and asks him to spend the rainy season in his own city, with the monks. The awakened, the Buddha answers, delight in quiet places. Understood, says the merchant. The texts call him Anathapindika. Today, the price he paid for a quiet place.
screen: `A HOUSE IN AN UPROAR.` → `THE BUDDHA IS COMING.` → `COME TO MY CITY.`

segments.voice: First, the place. Back home, Anathapindika looks for land for the monks: not too far from town, not too near, easy to reach, quiet at night. He finds it, a grove belonging to Prince Jeta, and asks to buy it. Second, the price. The prince doesn't want to sell, and says, more or less, not even if you covered it in gold coins. Then it's sold, says Anathapindika. The prince protests that he named no such deal. The Vinaya says they took it to the officials who settled such matters, and the officials ruled that a price had been named. Third, the gold. Anathapindika has gold brought out in carts and laid across the ground. One small patch near the gateway is still bare, and he sends for more. That's when the prince changes his mind. A man wouldn't spend like this, he thinks, unless the thing were truly worth it. He asks to give that last patch himself, and builds a gateway on it. So the place carries two names: Jeta's grove, Anathapindika's park. Fourth, the gift. Anathapindika builds dwellings, halls, storerooms and wells. When he asks how he should give it, the Buddha tells him to give it to the sangha of the four directions, those present and those still to come. Sutta after sutta opens with that place in its first line: the Blessed One was staying at Savatthi, in Jeta's grove, Anathapindika's park. Discourse after discourse, framed by one man's gold and one prince's gateway.
screen: `THE PRINCE'S GROVE.` · `NOT EVEN FOR GOLD.` · `CARTS OF COINS, ONE BARE PATCH.` · `FOR THE SANGHA OF FOUR DIRECTIONS.` · then, large: `COVERED IN GOLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give something generously. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you could give today: some time, a meal, some money, your full attention, a tool you never use. Then watch for the small pull to keep a patch bare, to give a little less than you first meant. You don't have to fight it. Just see it, the way Anathapindika saw the bare ground by the gate. Then decide on one gift, and decide it whole. Rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Gold coins on the ground. Anathapindika covers Prince Jeta's grove with gold to buy it for the monks, and the prince gives the last patch himself. Today's word.
screen: `GOLD COINS ON THE GROUND — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: covered in gold. Today, give your one gift all the way to the gate, without holding back the last bit. Day seven hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: In Buddhist communities lay people support monasteries with gifts of land, buildings, food and robes; giving a dwelling to the sangha is a traditional act of merit, and the story of Jeta's grove is retold when such gifts are made.

original.note: Pali Jetavana: Jeta's grove, the park at Savatthi that Anathapindika bought for the monks.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rich man showing off with his money.
what it means: a gift given so completely that even the seller is moved to give, and handed to the whole sangha, present and to come.
what a scholar hears: the Vinaya's Cullavagga tells the purchase; the suttas keep naming the place in their opening lines, Jeta's grove, Anathapindika's park.

notes: Cullavagga 6.4 paraphrased throughout. Confirm: the brother-in-law's preparations and Anathapindika's questions (wedding, sacrifice, king invited); his request that the Buddha spend the rains at Savatthi; the qualities of the site (not too far, not too near, quiet); Jeta's refusal 'not even for a covering of koti'; the officials' ruling; carts of gold; the bare patch by the gateway; Jeta's reflection and his gift of the gateway; the buildings listed; the Buddha's instruction to give it to the sangha of the four quarters, present and to come.
Amounts of gold (the commentaries give a figure in crores) are deliberately not stated.
'Open the suttas and that place keeps turning up in the first lines' is a general statement about many sutta openings set at Jetavana; confirm phrasing is acceptable under the claims rule.
The name Anathapindika is not explained (its usual explanation is commentarial).
Editor: review line made grammatical; the 'keeps turning up' sentence kept as a description of sutta openings (no count); no factual changes needed.

Auditor: hook corrected to the Cullavagga's actual request (that the Buddha spend the rains at Savatthi; 'Tathagatas delight in empty places'), not a request to give the monks a place; cut 'a gift that left no ground uncovered', which contradicted the prince's bare patch, and the overstated 'a whole teaching life'.
